# SK2201 — The unsubscription passes an anonymous function

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`-=` or `-` is applied to an event or a delegate with a lambda or an anonymous method on the right, and a delegate instance created here can never equal one created anywhere else, so the removal removes nothing.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

⚠ **This is not a heuristic. It is always true.** Delegate removal compares invocation-list entries by target and method, and an anonymous function written at one syntax site is a different instance from one written at any other — so `changed -= (s, e) => Redraw();` cannot remove the handler that `changed += (s, e) => Redraw();` added, however identical the two lines read. The subscription survives, the publisher keeps the subscriber alive for as long as it lives, and the line written to prevent the leak documents it instead. It is the shape that survives review precisely because it looks like the cleanup it is not.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
source.Changed += (s, e) => Redraw();
source.Changed -= (s, e) => Redraw();   // removes nothing
```

Write:

```csharp
EventHandler handler = (s, e) => Redraw();
source.Changed += handler;
source.Changed -= handler;
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **A method group is correct and is never reported.** `changed -= Handle` does remove what `changed += Handle` added, because two delegates over the same target and method compare equal; the defect belongs to anonymous functions specifically, and the rule says so by matching only lambda and anonymous-method nodes rather than by testing anything about them. A cast or parentheses around the anonymous function are unwrapped first, since `(EventHandler)(…)` changes the spelling and not the identity. ⚠ **The left operand's type is read, which is what keeps the rule off arithmetic.** It fires only where the left side binds to a delegate type — an event, or a delegate-typed field, local, parameter or property — so a `-=` on a number, or on an operand whose type did not resolve, is never examined. An anonymous function could not appear on the right of those and still compile, so this check is belt and braces rather than the rule; it is what makes the rule semantic. ⚠ **There is no fix, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** Repairing this means giving the delegate a name and storing it somewhere both the subscription and the unsubscription can reach, which changes the subscribing method and usually the type's fields as well — three edits away from this line, in places the diagnostic cannot see. An edit that merely deleted the `-=` would remove the author's stated intent to unsubscribe and leave the leak in place, which is worse than the finding. Generated code is excluded.
